articles.content: Woodward Plans to Transition Its Santa Clarita, California, Woodward Plans to Transition Its Santa Clarita, California, Aerospace Controls Production to Spartanburg, South Carolina Military controls production will move to the company’s new, state-of-the-art Spartanburg site; smaller, select product lines are under agreement to be sold, along with the Santa Clarita campus FORT COLLINS, Colo., Sept. 21, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Woodward, Inc. (NASDAQ: WWD), a world leader in aerospace and industrial control solutions, today announced its plans to transition production out of its Santa Clarita, California, facility to streamline its portfolio and refine its manufacturing footprint. Production of military fixed-wing and rotorcraft flight control actuation will move to Woodward's world-class aerospace manufacturing campus in Spartanburg, South Carolina, which is currently in advanced stages of construction. Separately, Woodward has agreed to sell a smaller group of legacy commercial rotorcraft, land systems, and business jet products made in Santa Clarita, along with the campus itself, in a transaction expected to close in fiscal year 2027. "We don't make decisions like this without recognizing what they mean for the people affected. Our team in Santa Clarita has contributed to Woodward for 17 years, and we are committed to supporting them through the transition with respect,” said Shawn McLevige, President of Woodward’s Aerospace segment. “This decision is in line with our strategy to continue creating value for our company and our shareholders through growth, operational excellence, and innovation. Moving this production to Spartanburg will help refine our manufacturing footprint to best support our customers and improve our supply chain as we meet increasing demand for industry-leading controls on current and next-generation commercial and military aircraft.” Woodward is expected to cease operations at the Santa Clarita facility no later than December 2027. The decision is expected to affect about 400 roles at the facility, with phased transitions through the planned move. The Spartanburg facility is expected to go online in the summer of 2027 and as previously announced, will produce Airbus A350 spoiler actuation systems, in addition to the transferred product lines and other aerospace components. Woodward is the global leader in the design, manufacture, and service of energy conversion and control solutions for the aerospace and industrial equipment markets. Our purpose is to design and deliver energy control solutions our partners count on to power a clean future. Our innovative fluid, combustion, electrical, propulsion, and motion control systems perform in some of the world’s harshest environments. Woodward is a global company headquartered in Fort Collins, Colorado, USA. articles.desc: Fed's Collins pencils in second hike this year, then expects rates on hold in 2027 Nasdaq Composite closes at a record as Meta and chip stocks surge Trump proposes USD 5 billion fund to help rebuild Gulf energy sites — WSJ St. Louis Fed’s Musalem: Interest rates likely need to rise further to tame i
articles.content: Fed's Collins pencils in second hike this year, then expects rates on hold in 2027 Nasdaq Composite closes at a record as Meta and chip stocks surge Trump proposes USD 5 billion fund to help rebuild Gulf energy sites — WSJ St. Louis Fed’s Musalem: Interest rates likely need to rise further to tame inflation Meta shares surge more than 10% as Muse excitement triggers a major technical breakout BOC’s Macklem: It could take some time for higher fuel margins to normalise Expect the News Headlines from Trump and the administration to be fast and furious going into the elections Bank of Canada’s Macklem: US tariffs could roughly halve fourth-quarter growth to below 1% Yemen President spoke to Trump but Trump made no pledge of military support Morning Kickstart: Oil slides as Middle East supply fears ease and risk appetite improves investingLive European session wrap: Oil extends fall, Bitcoin jumps to highest since January The Nasdaq closed at a record on Monday as Meta’s rally helped lift shares of Intel, AMD and Arm. At the same time, oil moved sharply lower. October light crude fell 4.87% to $95.42, while Brent moved above and below $100 and was near $100.05 in the supplied snapshot. The contrast sums up the session. Investors embraced the AI trade, but a pullback in oil eased some immediate energy inflation concerns. Three Fed officials still argued that inflation could require further action. The dollar was mixed to mostly higher, and Treasury yields fell beyond the short end of the curve. Foreign exchange was mixed with a tilt to the upside. The USD gained against the EUR, JPY, GBP, CAD and NZD. It was little changed against the AUD and slipped modestly against the CHF. The dollar’s largest gain among the currencies shown was against the JPY: USDJPY was near 157.39, up 0.34%. USDCAD was also up 0.34%, near 1.4034. The CHF was strongest against the dollar, although its gain was small. U.S. Treasury yields see the yield curve flatten A snap shot of the US debt market yield curve showed: 2-year: 4.7505%, up 0.75 basis points 5-year: 4.8271%, down 2.49 basis points 10-year: 4.9510%, down 4.50 basis points 30-year: 5.2803%, down 4.67 basis points The 2-year yield edged higher, but the rest of the curve moved lower. For a beginner trader, that means the bond market was not treating the Fed’s hawkish comments as a reason to push all yields higher. The drop in oil may have helped temper longer-term inflation concerns, though one day’s price action cannot settle that question. U.S. stocks: AI shares lead Dow Industrial Average: 52,054.19, up 366.04 points (+0.71%) S&P 500: 7,764.69, up 114.18 points (+1.49%) Nasdaq Composite: 27,122.09, up 599.55 points (+2.26%) to a record close Russell 2000: 2,875.3602, up 14.9636 points (+0.52%) Nasdaq 100: 30,482.35, up 838.19 points (+2.83%) Meta’s rally spreads to chips Meta’s move was the headline, but it was far from the only winner. The chip gains were even larger in some cases: Meta: up about 12%, its best day since January 29 Arm Holdings: $322.90, up 17.16% Intel: $121.81, up 12.17% AMD: $615.52, up 9.95%. AMD crossed $1 trillion in market value during the session. Meta’s surge was the standout stock story. Enthusiasm around its Muse AI assistant spread to semiconductor companies that investors see as potential beneficiaries of AI demand, including Intel, AMD and Arm. It is a reminder to look beneath the index headline. The Nasdaq’s record tells us buyers were in control of that index today, but the particularly strong moves in AI-related shares tell us where much of the excitement was concentrated. European stocks close higher across the board. European markets also finished higher helped by the rise in US stocks: Germany’s DAX: 25,575.02, up 270.95 points (+1.07%) France’s CAC 40: 8,138.95, up 73.92 points (+0.92%) U.K.’s FTSE 100: 10,739.02, up 79.88 points (+0.75%) Spain’s IBEX 35: 19,724.41, up 210.60 points (+1.08%) Italy’s FTSE MIB: 52,371.53, up 826.29 points (+1.60%) Italy led on a percentage basis, followed by Spain and Germany. Fed officials are not ready to declare victory St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said interest rates likely need to rise further to bring inflation under control. He sees both demand and supply pressures and favors earlier, smaller hikes over waiting and potentially needing larger moves later. Boston Fed President Susan Collins said she had penciled in another hike this year and expects rates to remain on hold in 2027. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said persistent supply shocks, including energy costs and tariffs, could require higher rates even if the resulting slowdown hurts employment. He also suggested that strong demand, including AI data center investment, could mean the Fed has more work to do. The question is whether inflation is being driven mainly by supply disruptions or by demand that remains too strong. A sustained drop in oil could help with the first problem. It would do less to resolve the second. The supplied material put the market-implied chance of an October Fed hike at about 55%. Oil and the Middle East October light crude fell $4.88, or 4.87%, to $95.42. Brent was down $3.82, or 3.68%, near $100.05 in the snapshot after trading on both sides of the $100 mark. The decline provided some relief after the recent rise in energy prices tied to the Middle East conflict. Still, Fed officials made clear today that they are concerned about inflation pressures extending beyond oil. Traders will want to see whether crude’s pullback holds and whether disruptions to the region’s energy infrastructure and transport routes continue to threaten supply. Gold, silver fall but Bitcoin is a big gainer on the day Gold was near $4,341.84, down 0.81%, while silver was near $65.96, down 0.40%. Gold fell even though longer-term Treasury yields declined, a move that would ordinarily offer it some support. The modestly firmer dollar may have been a headwind, but the supplied prices do not point to a single clear cause. Bitcoin stood near $86,915, up 7.10%. That was a much larger move than the daily changes across the major currencies and metals, and it came alongside strength in technology shares. What traders take into Tuesday The Nasdaq record, the nearly 5% slide in U.S. crude and the Fed’s inflation debate are the three stories to carry forward. Buyers had their shot in AI shares and followed through. Oil’s decline gave inflation watchers some breathing room. The Fed officials’ comments, however, show why one down day in crude is unlikely to end the rate debate. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

articles.desc: The Bottom Line: This week’s edition of the weekly restaurant finance newsletter examines the bankruptcy of Meritage Hospitality Group, one of the biggest franchise bankruptcies in years.
articles.content: Another major franchisee files for bankruptcy LeBron James invests in another restaurant chain A big Wendy's franchisee has declared bankruptcy. | Photo: Shutterstock This is from the weekly restaurant finance newsletter The Bottom Line. To get this in your inbox every Monday morning, This has been a tough run for Wendy’s. Management changes. Maybe-maybe-not deal ideas from Nelson Peltz. Falling sales. No longer bigger than Burger King. Now this: One of its biggest franchisees, Meritage Hospitality Group, has filed for bankruptcy. The Chapter 11 filing seems mostly straightforward. Wendy’s sales fell. The operator’s profitability followed suit. The company struggled with debt payments. It hired a restructuring expert. It decided on bankruptcy. Meritage is not a small bankruptcy. It is the largest, by far, since the 2020 filing of NPC International, also a Wendy’s operator but known more for its Pizza Hut ownership. It’s the type of bankruptcy filing that should cause brands to rethink how they franchise. Franchisee bankruptcies have taken off this year, and this one should shine a big light on the problems with operators right now. And it should discourage franchises from encouraging operators to amass large numbers of stores. In the fast-food space, franchisors have spent years putting more costs onto their operators, including technology fees, remodel costs, and expansion demands. Rising costs for food and labor led to soaring inflation, which prompted a discount war that is in its third year. Many franchisors did themselves little favor by courting large-scale operators under the idea that these franchisees had more financial wherewithal. But when such operators collapse, they create massive problems for the brand. With one bankruptcy, Meritage put 5% of Wendy’s U.S. locations under Chapter 11. That’s a big problem. Regardless, brands need to maintain a focus on franchisee profitability regardless of the size of their operators. The future of their systems depend on it. Pizza Hut has been sold and of course its new private-equity owners are using a whole business securitization to finance the deal. I’m sure that there will be no problems at all whatsoever. But the economy is going well enough that the Fed is raising interest rates , which is good I guess. But fast-food restaurants haven’t been participating in the party. That’s bad. Restaurant Brands International settled a lawsuit over its 2024 Carrols deal Dave & Buster’s doesn’t think the economy is its problem anymore A big Domino’s now-former franchisee closed 13 locations . But folks tell me they expect those locations to reopen quickly. Sailormen, the other big franchisee bankruptcy this year, is suing a company that backed out of an agreement to take over some of its restaurants. Domino’s closures have been paltry for years, at less than half a percent every year, which is what happens when you make $1.4 million per store in a model that works roughly anywhere. “It hasn’t really changed my habits, because you can always take half your meal home or, frankly, my boyfriend usually eats the rest.” - Karen Pagonis, a GLP-1 user, on her restaurant habits. articles.title: A big Wendy's bankruptcy reveals the chain's challenges
articles.desc: The Bottom Line: The Chapter 11 filing of Meritage Hospitality Group was the biggest filing by a restaurant franchisee in six years. The company points the blame squarely at the franchisor.
articles.content: A big Wendy's bankruptcy reveals the chain's challenges LeBron James invests in another restaurant chain Wendy's sales problems, and rising beef costs, hit Meritage Hospitality hard. | Photo: Shutterstock Meritage Hospitality Group, one of the biggest franchisees in the Wendy’s system, . In the process, it painted a stark picture of the challenges facing not only Wendy's operators but also franchisees across many other restaurant systems. The Grand Rapids, Michigan-based company filed for bankruptcy with 320 locations, all but six of them Wendy’s units. That makes it the biggest bankruptcy by a restaurant franchisee since NPC International six years ago. Court documents and other filings reveal a company that took on an enormous amount of debt to buy, open, and remodel locations. It also relied heavily on a beverage contract rebate for a large amount of its profits. When that rebate vanished and Wendy’s sales fell, the franchisee’s business sunk. Kevin Cleary, Meritage’s chief restructuring officer, in a court filing on Saturday blamed the bankruptcy on “a convergence of external factors.” Cleary cited the “reduced frequency and effectiveness of Wendy’s brand marketing under prior franchisor management.” Last year, Wendy’s front-loaded its marketing budget, which hurt sales toward the end of 2025. But the company’s same-store sales have fallen more than 10% on a two-year basis in the first half of this year, which makes it clear that the brand’s marketing has not been effective. Cleary also blamed winter weather, which “created highly disruptive impacts on sales.” On top of that, the company faced a combination of soaring beef costs and an environment in which the fast-food business was competing largely on price. Cleary said that beef costs at Wendy’s rose 18.9%. He also cited “margin compression resulting from deep discounting and national promotional strategies at the brand level.” In presentations earlier this year, Meritage suggested that Wendy’s was more reliant on beef than competitors, notably McDonald’s. Meritage noted that 50% of McDonald’s protein sales come from beef, while at Wendy’s 80% of its sales come from beef, making the company more reliant on a product whose costs have taken off this year. This, in a nutshell, is the problem in the Wendy’s system, and many others. A three-year price war has coincided with soaring costs to create problems at a company that used large amounts of debt to buy, build, and remodel restaurants. Meritage was originally founded in 1986 as a hotel operating platform. But it ditched that idea more than a decade later and opted to focus on the fast-food business, specifically with Wendy’s. It has since spent the years mostly buying Wendy’s units. At one point it operated more than 370 locations of the fast-food chain, though it recently started getting into the Bojangles business, opening its first location of the chicken chain last year. It also has a handful of independent restaurants. The company has closed 60 Wendy’s units this year. Meritage has a lot of secured debt — about $155 million worth. As revenues began to decline, that debt was a bigger problem. But so were its royalty payments. Revenues at the company fell 7.6% to $688.8 million, according to court documents. But they’d fallen further, down 14%, in the first half of this year. Meritage reported a $31.5 million net loss last year, and that was worsening this year. The company’s net loss was $23.1 million so far in 2026. Not mentioned in the court documents, but raised in prior filings and investor presentations by Meritage, was an issue with Wendy’s beverage contract with Coca-Cola. Wendy’s under Kirk Tanner renegotiated that contract, which lowered the prices operators paid for their soda. Yet Meritage did not receive $11 million in rebates earlier this year, which during normal years amounts to a quarter of the company’s annual EBITDA, or earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization. articles.content: ‘Macbeth’ will open Met Opera season with an unexpected director - WSB-TV Channel 2 - Atlanta Louisa Proske’s Met debut will be ‘Macbeth,’ ‘a terrifying tale for terrifying times’ NEW YORK — It's less than a 40-minute walk uptown to the Metropolitan Opera House from where got its humble start in a yoga studio. But for Louisa Proske, it's been an artistic journey years in the making. Proske, who co-founded the scrappy company in 2014, is making her Met debut in the highest-profile assignment imaginable: opening the season directing a new production of Verdi’s “Macbeth” with an all-star cast. The job came her way less than a year ago after another director bowed out. Planning for new productions typically starts two or more years in advance. “I was aware of Louisa’s success at Heartbeat, and she had been on my radar,” Met general manager Peter Gelb said. “In terms of who was available on relatively short notice, Louisa was an obvious choice.” As Proske recalled her conversation with Gelb, “He said, ‘Can you do it very, very fast? The design was due yesterday.’” “I said it’s a big challenge,” she added. “But I love impossible challenges.” Impossible challenges are nothing new for Proske She had plenty of those at Heartbeat, which developed a reputation for reimagining the classics in eye-opening ways while operating on a shoestring budget. Luckily she was able to recruit partners she had already worked with: costume designer Montana Levi Blanco and set designer Jon Bausor — both with previous Met experience — and choreographer Jorrell Lawyer-Jefferson. “That sealed the deal,” she said. It also helped that Proske was intimately familiar with the Shakespeare play, having written her thesis on it at the University of Cambridge. Now for the past few weeks, she has put her knowledge and imagination to work, immersing her cast — which includes a contingent of dancing witches — in what she calls “a terrifying tale for terrifying times.” A Met newcomer who took charge like a veteran And if she felt any trepidation about taking on such a huge challenge at a huge house, it wasn’t apparent in rehearsal. “If this had been my first outing with the Met, I would have guessed that she’d been working here for at least a few years,” said baritone Quinn Kelsey, who portrays Macbeth. “She doesn’t come in there like a drill sergeant, but when she needs everyone’s attention, she gets it. “It’s obvious she’s excited,” he said, “and wanting to show us all these wonderful ideas she’s come up with for us to portray our characters.” as Banquo. Met music director Yannick Nezet-Seguin conducts the orchestra and chorus in the production, which opens Tuesday and runs for 10 performances. The Saturday matinee on Oct. 17 will be broadcast live to movie theaters around the world. To Proske the opera is about “the corrupt lust for power, the disintegration of the society, the slide into tyranny, all things that I think Shakespeare wrote very acutely about. “I think it expresses the agony of living in times that you don’t really understand anymore,” she continued. “That it only takes three steps for all guardrails to be gone, the world descending into total savagery and bloodshed. And I do think this is a very current sentiment.” She has taken inspiration from Verdi’s remark that the story has three major characters: Macbeth, Lady Macbeth — and the witches, who in this production act as what Proske called “greedy voyeurs of the Macbeths’ descent into crime and bloodshed.” “Sometimes they just lurk in the shadows, and you have a sense that they’re there,” she said. “Almost like insects, or mold, they sort of creep through the walls, more and more invading those spaces as rules are broken and values transgressed.” Bausor’s set suggests a modern war-torn landscape, with a false proscenium like a giant concrete wall with a huge hole blasted through it and rubble piled at the sides. articles.content: The prices of the latest iPhones are higher than ever , but there’s some good news for people who bought some models that are a few years older: Apple may owe you up to $95. That’s because in May, the company agreed to settle a lawsuit alleging it misled customers about the AI capabilities of select iPhones sold in 2024 and 2025. Now people who say they were impacted can finally make a claim. Here’s what you need to know. What is the settlement about? The settlement centers on a class action lawsuit alleging that Apple advertised certain artificial intelligence features for its Siri AI chatbot on the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 models that the company failed to ship in a timely manner. The class action alleges that consumers were harmed by these undelivered Siri promises because they bought an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 model expecting specific Apple Intelligence AI features within a certain timeframe. Such features included Siri on-screen awareness, which Apple originally previewed in June of 2024, when the iPhone 15 Pro was still the company’s flagship device. That fall, when Apple announced the new iPhone 16 series, it said Siri’s on-screen awareness features would arrive by early 2025. In reality, Apple kept pushing back the rollout. On-screen Siri AI awareness ultimately arrived on the iPhone with the release of iOS 27 earlier this month. That’s around 18 months after Apple initially said the feature would roll out. Apple was sued by people who bought the iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 series due to these delayed features. Instead of entering a costly legal battle, Apple in May agreed to settle the lawsuit for $250 million, while admitting no wrongdoing. This week, the settlement website launched its official claims form, which means people who say they were impacted by the delayed Siri AI features can finally file a a claim seeking part of the $250 million settlement fund. Who is included in the Siri Apple Intelligence settlement? In order to be eligible to make a claim for a portion of the $250 million settlement, you must meet the following criteria, according to the official settlement website : You must be living in the United States. You must have purchased an eligible iPhone (see below) in the United States. You must have purchased that eligible iPhone between June 10, 2024, and March 29, 2025. You must be the original purchaser of the device. The device must have been purchased for personal or business use, and not for resale. Which iPhones are included in the settlement? Eligible iPhone models covered under this settlement include the following: iPhone 15 Pro iPhone 15 Pro Max iPhone 16 iPhone 16e iPhone 16 Plus iPhone 16 Pro iPhone 16 Pro Max Other iPhones are not covered by the settlement. How much can I get from the settlement? The settlement saw Apple agree to pay $250 million. However, some of that money will go toward compensating the lawyers representing the class action plaintiffs and covering court costs. The remaining funds will be distributed to those covered by the settlement. According to the settlement website, individuals who file a successful claim will receive a payment of $25. However, that payment may increase significantly, depending on how many people file a claim. The maximum amount people who file a successful claim can expect is $95. The final amount will not be known until after the claim submission window has closed. How do I get my share of the Siri Apple Intelligence settlement? In order to receive a payment from the settlement funds, affected individuals must file a claim. Claims can be filed online . Claimants are urged to read the full details on the official settlement website to determine whether they qualify for a payment. But potential claimants need to act fast. Claim submissions open today, Monday, September 21. But the claim window is relatively short. Eligible individuals must file a claim by December 21, 2026—just three months from today.

articles.title: Two Utah Firms Are Building the Nets and Swarms of Next-Gen Drone Warfare
articles.desc: Lindon's Fortem Technologies and Bluffdale's Vector are building counter-drone nets and attritable drones for the Pentagon and 2026 World Cup security.
articles.content: Utah Drone Warfare Companies: Fortem and Vector Explained Two Utah Firms Are Building the Nets and Swarms of Next-Gen Drone Warfare 1855 W 500 N — Fortem Technologies Utah Base Utah companies are developing two different pieces of the emerging counter-drone system: Fortem Technologies builds radar-guided interceptors that physically capture drones, while Bluffdale startup Vector makes and trains users on systems intended for increasingly autonomous operations. Their work reflects a broader effort to detect, track and neutralize small, relatively inexpensive drones before they can endanger people or disrupt critical sites. A Radar Company That Became a Net-Firing Drone Hunter Fortem Technologies began as a company building radar systems for drone delivery before pivoting into compact, high-performance radar and drone autonomy systems, according to . That evolution produced the DroneHunter F700, a fully autonomous, radar-guided interceptor that Fortem says has made nearly 5,000 drone captures, per the company's own product materials on . The system is built around three product families — TrueView sensors, SkyDome Manager software and the DroneHunter interceptors themselves — that work together to spot, track and physically capture threats. The capture mechanism is more net than missile. The F700 is armed with multiple NetGuns and what Fortem calls a DrogueNet, and KSL reports the aircraft snags drones with a 3-meter-by-3-meter net before flying the captured drone to a safe location. Fortem founder and chief technology officer Adam Robertson described the process to KSL, saying the DroneHunter “pursues evasive targets and captures them with an onboard-radar-guided net.” Fortem's own site adds that large captured drones are forced into a slow, safe descent, while smaller ones are towed to a location the operator selects — a nonlethal alternative to shooting a hostile drone out of the sky. From International Events to the 2026 World Cup Fortem's technology has already been used to protect major international events. The company was contracted to intercept attack drones at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, as reported by both . For the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security placed a multimillion-dollar order for Fortem systems at 11 U.S. venues, according to unmannedsystemstechnology.com. Breaking Defense reports that Fortem will deploy DroneHunter systems at 11 World Cup venues starting June 11, 2026. Robertson told KSL that DroneHunter technology has already been deployed as a security measure around FIFA World Cup sites, and he expects that kind of protection to become more routine. “Drone protection is going to become more fundamental worldwide,” Robertson said, per KSL's report. He pointed to a widening list of potential targets beyond stadiums — dams, power stations, capitol buildings and data centers — as reasons counter-drone systems are moving from novelty to necessity. Fortem also supplies the U.S. military and overseas allies with DroneHunter systems and radar equipment, and the company has received a U.S. government Air Force research grant, KSL reports. Swarms, Autonomy and a New Kind of Coordination Beyond single interceptions, coordinated drone defense is an emerging focus in the industry. That vision lines up with where the broader industry is headed. Andy Yakulis, a Vector co-founder who served roughly 18 years in the U.S. Army as a helicopter pilot and special operations forces member, told KSL that drone warfare technology is moving toward full autonomy. He described future drone operations involving multiple groups of drones at once — a shift toward swarms augmented by artificial intelligence, where AI or autonomy controls multiple groups of drones simultaneously. articles.content: Getech: Yorkshire-based subsurface research firm seeing increased demand due to drive for energy security Getech: Yorkshire-based subsurface research firm seeing increased demand due to drive for energy security Yorkshire-based subsurface research firm Getech has said it is seeing a boost in demand for its services on the back of an increased focus from governments on energy security. , locates subsurface resources for industries including oil and gas and natural hydrogen. Announcing its first-half year results, the company hailed a positive outlook as it cited a number of market tailwinds. CEO, said in a statement: “Industry conditions continue to support a strengthening exploration outlook, driven by persistently low reserve replacement among the supermajors, a longer oil-demand horizon and an increased focus on energy security and geographic diversification. “This requirement for long-term energy supply is driving both established and emerging energy resource opportunities, creating demand for the data, specialised software and geoscience expertise needed to assess new geographies and resources efficiently. “Getech’s core markets of oil & gas, mining and natural hydrogen have all seen increased activity, which we expect to be reflected in the group’s future performance given our proven ability to identify and de-risk new exploration projects.” Mr Jepps added that the company was entering the second half “in a much stronger position than previous years”. It comes at a time in which countries across the world are making moves to improve energy security, following widespread industry shocks due to the wars in Ukraine and continues to face looming decisions on whether to approve the controversial Jackdaw and Rosebank fields in the North Sea. Announcing its results for the six months ended June 30, Getech posted revenues of £2.4m, up from £2.1m a year prior. The firm also narrowed its pre-tax losses significantly, landing at £241,000, down from £914,000 in the same period a year prior. Getech posted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation for the period of £232,000, up from a loss of £196,000. Michael Covington, Getech chairman, said: “The first half of 2026 has been an important step forward for Getech. “We delivered profitable EBITDA, improved cash generation and strengthened our recurring revenue base, whilst continuing to invest in the proprietary data and technologies that differentiate the company. “Our largely fixed cost base provides the potential for meaningful operational leverage as revenues expand.” Iconic Media Group Ltd. articles.title: Bruker Receives Order for High-Field NMR Systems for Major Upgrade of Magnetic Resonance Research Infrastructure at UC Berkeley
articles.content: Bruker Receives Order for High-Field NMR Systems for Major Upgrade of Magnetic Resonance Research Infrastructure at UC Berkeley - BioSpace Bruker Receives Order for High-Field NMR Systems for Major Upgrade of Magnetic Resonance Research Infrastructure at UC Berkeley New high-field NMR instrumentation strengthens biomolecular and materials science research at the UC Berkeley Pines Magnetic Resonance Center (Nasdaq: BRKR) today announced a multi-system order from the for high-field Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) instrumentation at the Pines Magnetic Resonance Center. The investment will enhance access to next-generation NMR technologies, including 800 MHz–class instrumentation. These capabilities strengthen research in chemistry, materials science, structural biology, and related fields across UC Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. The Pines Magnetic Resonance Center (PMRC) comprises faculty, technical staff, and postdoctoral researchers. The PMRC Core NMR facility is a leading shared NMR resource, offering 24/7 access to researchers from academia, national laboratories, and industry. By integrating high-performance instrumentation with method development, training, and analytical services, the facility enables multidisciplinary studies of molecular structure, dynamics, and function. The investment is centered on a Bruker AV NEO-X 800 MHz spectrometer equipped with a cryogenically cooled MAS CryoProbe, complemented by several additional NMR systems and upgrades supporting solid-state, solution-state and Dynamic Nuclear Polarization (DNP) research. “This expansion will propel UC Berkeley, an institution with an exceptionally strong tradition in magnetic resonance, to the forefront of high-impact innovation for years to come,” said Professor Tatyana Polenova, Director of the Pines Magnetic Resonance Center. “By integrating next-generation NMR and DNP with advanced methodologies, including fast magic-angle spinning, MAS CryoProbes, computational analysis, and quantum sensing and control, we are opening new avenues to address previously inaccessible structural and mechanistic questions across a broad range of systems, including intact cells and organisms, macromolecular assemblies, bio-inspired materials, inorganic materials, and molecules at interfaces and surfaces.” “Translating cutting-edge NMR technologies into robust, reproducible workflows is critical,” said Dr. Patrick Wikus, Head of Product Management at Bruker BioSpin. “The AV NEO-X platform provides a robust foundation for advanced solid-state, solution-state, and DNP NMR experiments, combining highest performance and enabling new capabilities with reliable day-to-day operation.” The UC Berkeley NMR order exceeds $6 million and is expected to be delivered in 2027. In close cooperation with our customers, Bruker is enabling innovation, improved productivity, and customer success in post-genomic life science molecular and cell biology research, in applied and biopharma applications, in microscopy, as well as in industrial and cleantech research, and semiconductor metrology in support of AI.
